title: 'Putney pusher' suspect found dead at home
description: A spokesperson for the force said officers attended the property in Chiswick alongside paramedics "after a man was found unresponsive"."Sadly, a 44-ye
body: A spokesperson for the force said officers attended the property in Chiswick alongside paramedics "after a man was found unresponsive"."Sadly, a 44-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene. His next-of-kin have been informed," they said. Brandram, who served as a Captain in the Scots Guards in Afghanistan, was working more recently in private banking for HSBC.He is known to been a distant relative of European royalty - his grandmother was Princess Katherine of Greece, and the late Duke of Edinburgh, Prince Philip, was his father's godfather.While in police custody in June over the Putney Bridge incident, Brandram was also arrested on suspicion of drug possession.Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

title: Earl Spencer's unreleased book on Diana stolen in the Netherlands
description: Copies of Earl Spencer's unreleased book on his sister Diana, Princess of Wales, have been stolen from a truck in the Netherlands.The BBC understands
body: Copies of Earl Spencer's unreleased book on his sister Diana, Princess of Wales, have been stolen from a truck in the Netherlands.The BBC understands four copies of the Dutch language edition were taken from a truck while it was en route from the Dutch publisher's printers to their warehouse. Dutch police said they were aware of the incident and have been approached for comment.  Swan Song: Diana, My Sister is due to be released in the UK and globally on Tuesday, and tells the story of Princess Diana's life from the Earl's perspective. A source said the truck driver was taking a mandatory break in a car park and was sleeping in his cab at the time the books were stolen.They added Dutch police are investigating. They did not say where the theft took place. The Daily Mail, who first reported the theft, external and is serialising the book, said the theft took place earlier this week in the Dutch countryside. The book's publisher Penguin Michael Joseph - a division of Penguin Random House - and Dutch publisher Overamstel, who have rights to the book in the Netherlands, were approached for comment by the BBC. Princess Diana, who died aged 36 following a car crash in Paris in 1997, would have turned 65 on 1 July this year.Her sons Prince William and Prince Harry were aged 15 and 12 respectively at the time of her death.Last month announcing the book's publication, Earl Spencer explained ahead of the 30th anniversary of her death he had been inundated with interview requests and he wanted to write down his own thoughts and memories rather than "having the discomfort of again reading the opinions of others". "The aim of this book is to tell the truth about Diana from her brother's perspective, just as I attempted to do when speaking at her funeral," he added, referring to the eulogy he delivered in Westminster Abbey in September 1997."I want to speak on Diana's behalf and do so in an openly positive way."In his eulogy, Earl Spencer described Princess Diana as the "very essence of compassion, of duty, of style, of beauty", adding: "All over the world she was a symbol of selfless humanity... a standard bearer for the rights of the truly downtrodden."He also used the speech to criticise the media, calling her the "most hunted person of the modern age" and pledged to protect Prince William and Prince Harry and prevent them suffering a similar fate.In 2023, copies of Prince Harry's memoir Spare were accidentally put on sale in Spain days ahead of the official global release.

schema.headline: Earl Spencer's unreleased book on Diana stolen in the Netherlands

title: Andy Burnham and his chancellor have a battle on their hands
description: Today's inflation figures underscore that the economy is the biggest challenge facing Andy Burnham.It is only 42 days until John Healey's first Budget
body: Today's inflation figures underscore that the economy is the biggest challenge facing Andy Burnham.It is only 42 days until John Healey's first Budget, and there is increasingly apparent concern at all levels of the government and Labour Party about how that Budget can – or, as it may prove, cannot – substantiate Burnham's rhetoric about offering the biggest change in British politics in 40 years.Much of the tricky economic environment, yes, is driven by global factors including the persistence, and to some degree worsening, of the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine.And the AI boom pushing up borrowing costs is another issue affecting many countries.But there are clearly domestic factors particular to Britain, and on that front it was very striking to hear the former Bank of England chief economist Andy Haldane telling LBC on Tuesday that without signs of cuts to public spending "the markets now suspect that this is a traditional tax and spend socialist government with better TikTok videos".From somebody who at times has informally advised Burnham's operation, that will sting, not least because a similar criticism has been voiced in recent weeks by the prominent economist Lord O'Neill – another sometime adviser.The prime minister gave a direct response to Haldane, saying: "That doesn't tell the story. We are not that."He identified "putting digital ID on hold" as an example of how he had already "taken difficult decisions in this job in relation to reprioritising government spending" and vowed to continue to "take difficult decisions to make sure the economy remains on track".Digital ID is a striking choice of example. Burnham announced that he was abandoning the scheme in the days before he became prime minister so that he could focus on policies affecting the everyday cost of living. But the spending was then, within the new government's first few days, re-allocated to cut VAT on household electricity bills.So in that sense it was not a reduction in public spending, just a reprioritisation. And in any case, the former cabinet minister Darren Jones criticised Burnham at the time on the grounds that the government had not yet allocated the money for digital ID.Certainly the signs from Healey's first major speech as chancellor last week were that he wants to reassure the markets, promising to "control public spending" and praising Rachel Reeves for beginning to "recover Britain's fiscal discipline".Burnham and Healey would hardly be the first PM-chancellor double act to adopt different tones and emphasise different priorities in their public appearances. As a junior minister at the Treasury almost 25 years ago, Healey was engaged in the question of how to boost growth around the country, long before it became central to Burnham's vision for Britain.But there are people in government who are beginning to wonder whether their economic visions are quite as aligned as expected. "It's what everyone is thinking and some of us are vocalising," one government source said.There are also those who fear the adverse political consequences of a Labour government seeking to go out of its way to demonstrate its fiscal credibility. Arguably that was behind the removal of the Winter Fuel Allowance for most pensioners as one of Sir Keir Starmer's first acts, an early factor in his political demise.For Labour's political opponents, all this amounts to a question of whether the prime minister is willing to disappoint his own MPs. Yet it's worth remembering that with winter fuel the frustration in parliament was primarily caused by the furious reaction of Labour MPs' constituents.Arguably this presents a more fundamental tension: are the kinds of policies needed to soothe the markets politically deliverable given Labour's electoral coalition and its need to shore up the 'progressive' vote?The Budget is only six weeks away and will be the first and most important sign of the new government's answer to that question.

schema.headline: Andy Burnham and his chancellor have a battle on their hands

title: Bonnie Greer: British-American author and critic dies at 77
description: Writer and broadcaster Bonnie Greer dies aged 77Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Greer's work often tackled topics around culture, race and pu
body: Writer and broadcaster Bonnie Greer dies aged 77Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Greer's work often tackled topics around culture, race and public institutionsByPaul GlynnCulture reporterBritish-American author and cultural commentator Bonnie Greer has died at the age of 77 after a brief illness, her husband has said.In a statement delivered with "profound sadness", Greer's widower David Hutchins noted how the acclaimed playwright and critic had made "an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life" with her "intelligence, courage and distinctive voice".He added: "To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her."Hutchins continued: "Those closest to Bonnie will remember her warmth, humour, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together."'Courage, humour and humanity'BBC presenter Clive Myrie led the tributes from elsewhere, posting on X: "This is such a shock. She was a friend and mentor and I will miss her with all my heart."Former deputy prime minister David Lammy called Greer "a powerful wordsmith and artist, she was eloquent and exacting".He added that she was "a true life force" and he would "never forget her quiet fearlessness taking on Nick Griffin" during an appearance with the then-British National Party leader on the BBC's Question Time in 2009.Lammy added: "I will miss her mentorship, and her friendship."London Mayor Sadiq Khan said Greer's voice brought "courage, humour and humanity to Britain's cultural conversation".He said: "She inspired and opened doors for so many others. And she was great fun too - I will miss her friendship enormously."Plays, novels and Question TimeBorn in Chicago in 1948, Greer wrote plays from a young age and went on to study theatre in her home city and before attending the Actors Studio in New York with director Elia Kazan.Greer moved to the UK in 1986 and became a familiar face on UK TV, appearing as a powerful panellist on programmes like Newsnight Review and Question Time.She penned award-winning works like Munda Negra, which won her the Verity Bargate Award for best play, and novels such as Hanging by Her Teeth (1994) and Entropy (2009).Once named by the Observer, external as one of the country's leading public intellectuals, Greer's work - across a range of disciplines and platforms - often tackled topics around culture, race and public institutions.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Greer was made an OBE for services to the arts in 2010Speaking to the Guardian, external in 2016 in the aftermath of the Black Lives Matter movement, Greer said: "When I wake up in the morning, I'm just myself. It's only when I leave the door that I become a black woman to the world."She added: "I tell black women all the time, 'Don't apologise for yourself and keep your hair nappy. Make sure you are heard'."Greer served on the boards of cultural institutions including the British Museum, Royal Opera House and London Film School, and was chancellor of London's Kingston University.Her other published works include a memoir titled A Parallel Life and a biography of US poet and playwright Langston Hughes.Also in 2009, her part-memoir, part-music-history book, Obama Music, was published.Greer was made an OBE in 2010 for services to the arts.In 2022, she was appointed as a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature.

schema.headline: Bonnie Greer: British-American author and critic dies at 77

title: Call to raising tax thresholds among union demands to Chancellor
description: Unions who donate to Labour will meet John Healey on Thursday to press home their demands ahead of next month's Budget.Unite, the UK's second biggest
body: Unions who donate to Labour will meet John Healey on Thursday to press home their demands ahead of next month's Budget.Unite, the UK's second biggest union, has called for a reversal of the freezing of tax thresholds, that see the lowest paid drawn into paying tax.The union's leader, Sharon Graham, said she told Andy Burnham that the cut to the  winter fuel allowance, carried out under former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, was a "disgrace", adding: "What to you need to do is winter fuel in reverse - something that says to everyday people I am on your side."The call is one of a number of policy proposals unions are taking to the chancellor, including increased taxes on tech companies.Unions say they believe Healey's first budget will define Andy Burnham's direction of travel as prime minister.Unite took legal action against Sir Keir's government when the winter fuel payment was restricted to the poorest pensioners, and Graham believed this policy - which was not in Labour's manifesto - was politically poisonous.Burnham said the freezing of tax thresholds had come up on the doorsteps when he was campaigning to return to Westminster as MP for Makerfield. In her last Budget, then-Chancellor Rachel Reeves froze tax thresholds until 2031. The basic rate of 20% is paid on annual earnings between £12,571 and £50,270. The higher rate of 40% is paid on earnings between £50,271 and £125,140.By not uprating those rates in line with inflation, more lower paid people have paid tax for the first time and more better-off workers, including public service workers such as senior nurses, police officers and teachers, are now paying tax at the higher rate.Graham said: "We must see things happen immediately. I told him [Burnham] that you have to make working class people believe their best days are in front of them. "That tax threshold of around £12,500 - if that hadn't been frozen for the past few years it would have moved up to over £16,000 now. People at the lower end are paying eye-watering amounts of tax."The country's biggest union Unison is calling for the chancellor to increase tax on large tech companies to finance public sector investment and the transition to green energy.It is also calling for the Treasury to commission research into whether the balance of taxation needs to move from income to wealth.The union's general secretary Andrea Egan is not expecting dramatic change from Healey straight away at the Budget, but is expecting a new direction to be mapped out.Her union is demanding that Labour makes clear it too is under new leadership and isn't just "continuity Starmer" with a more affable face.The third biggest union, GMB, also has significant financial links to the Labour Party.Leader Gary Smith has long advocated raising revenue from the oil and gas industries by approving the new Rosebank and Jackdaw fields in the North Sea. A decision on whether these will go ahead seems unlikely until after the October by election in Sir Keir's former seat in north London - though the government maintains the timing is out of its hands as it is a quasi judicial decision.Smith said: "The government really needs to get on with this. "We are going to need oil and gas for generations to come. Rosebank and Jackdaw are good for jobs, good for the economy,  but also good for the environment as we won't have to import so much from abroad as that is carbon intensive."Smith also wants to see confidence building measures for the construction industry in the Budget. He said: "We have half a million bricks stockpiled in this country - enough to build two Kidderminsters - and factories are being mothballed because we are not getting on with the house building programme. They have to cut through the red tape."In the next couple of weeks, TUC officials and representatives of those unions which don't donate to Labour will also meet the chancellor.TUC leader Paul Nowak told me his main demand was for Healey to reverse the last government's cut in the surcharge paid by banks to raise around £9bn to subsidise energy bills.But he also wants to see the remit of the independent Budget watchdog, the OBR, revised, so it takes into account the value of long term investment and not just short term book-balancing.

schema.headline: Call to raising tax thresholds among union demands to Chancellor

title: Vini Jnr, Mbappe and Konate obscure Ceuta message ahead of Real Madrid match
description: Kylian Mbappe, Vinicius Junior and Ibrahima Konate rolled up their pre-game T-shirts ahead of Real Madrid's match at Elche on Tuesday to obscure the m
body: Kylian Mbappe, Vinicius Junior and Ibrahima Konate rolled up their pre-game T-shirts ahead of Real Madrid's match at Elche on Tuesday to obscure the message of support for the people of Ceuta.Ceuta is a Spanish autonomous city on the North African coast, bordering Morocco and separated from mainland Spain by the Strait of Gibraltar.Players from both sides walked on to the pitch at Elche's ground, Martinez Valero, wearing white T-shirts carrying the message "Todos somos caballas" – translated as "We are all Ceutans" – along with references to the Spanish autonomous city.While most of the players wore the shirts fully, Mbappe, Vinicius and Konate had theirs rolled up to around chest height, obscuring some of the slogan.Mbappe and Vinicius then removed their shirts before the pre-match handshake, while Konate kept his on for longer. Their team-mates and the Elche players continued to wear the shirts through the pre-match formalities.This is not the first time Real Madrid have shown support for Ceuta. Before their Champions League meeting with Inter Milan at the Santiago Bernabeu on 8 September, supporters in the south stand displayed cards featuring the coat of arms of the autonomous city, while the rest of the stadium joined the tribute with a round of applause.The initiative was part of a wider show of support for Ceuta, following a major migration crisis in the Spanish territory after thousands of people entered from Morocco.At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July. Most swam around a border fence and at least 100 people died during the crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor.Although most returned, as many as 5,000 remain in makeshift camps or are sleeping on the city's streets and beaches, leading to unrest in the autonomous Spanish city in North Africa. Locals have expressed safety concerns and some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants.The representatives of the players have been asked for comment.The episode came shortly before a dramatic night for Real Madrid, who recovered from surrendering a two-goal lead to beat Elche 3-2, with Carlos Espi scoring the winner in stoppage time. Mbappe was among Madrid's scorers, while Vinicius started the game.The pre-match gesture also highlighted the differing approaches among players and clubs to the Ceuta campaign. Barcelona did not take part in the initiative, while players at other La Liga fixtures had worn the shirts as intended.

schema.headline: Vini Jnr, Mbappe and Konate obscure Ceuta message ahead of Real Madrid match

title: At least 21 killed after war-damaged Gaza building collapses
description: Eight children among 21 killed after war-damaged Gaza building collapses, rescuers sayFigure caption, Rescuers search for survivors with their bare ha
body: Eight children among 21 killed after war-damaged Gaza building collapses, rescuers sayFigure caption, Rescuers search for survivors with their bare handsByYolande KnellMiddle East correspondentReporting fromJerusalem and David GrittenUpdated 2 hours agoAt least 21 people have been killed, including eight children, and dozens are missing after a war-damaged building collapsed in the Gaza Strip overnight, local rescuers and medics say.Witnesses told the BBC that the six-storey building in the Tal al-Hawa area of Gaza City had been left tilting dangerously to one side after an Israeli strike more than a year ago. Displaced families were living inside because they were desperate, they said.UN agencies and an Egyptian team have joined the search for survivors, but officials say it is proceeding slowly due to a lack of equipment.In the initial rescue effort, members of the Hamas-run Civil Defence agency resorted to using their bare hands."We are still hearing voices from under the rubble, so there is still hope to find people," said Raed al-Dahshan, the director of the Civil Defence in Gaza City.He added: "The limited availability of shelter options forced residents to move into this building, believing it was safe. However, at one point it collapsed entirely, tragically crashing down on people as they slept."Image source, ReutersImage caption, Locals said about 10 families had been living in the building despite warnings that it was unsafeA woman living in a tent nearby, Umm Mohammed Bakrun, said she had been talking to her son when the building collapsed suddenly in the early hours of Wednesday."It felt like an earthquake. There was a loud sound and I couldn't stand up. Stones rained down on us and when I looked outside I saw a lot of dust," she told the BBC. "Within minutes, there were screams everywhere."Another witness, Mansour Abu Mohammed, said the building collapsed "in a few seconds"."Every day, a stone or a few stones would fall from it, but the people inside couldn't find anywhere else to live. I used to live next door to it and you could see that it was tilting to one side."Locals said some 10 families had been living in the building's apartments.Satellite imagery shows that the area around the building was targeted in the early weeks of the war, while damage to the building itself first became evident in 2024.The head of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Gaza office, Alessandro Mrakic, told reporters at the scene that between 70 and 100 people were believed to be trapped under the rubble."The situation, as you see, is tragic because we don't have the equipment and machinery that is needed. There are actually people digging with their bare hands," he said.Mrakic also warned that approximately 400 other war-damaged buildings across Gaza were at imminent risk of collapse, particularly as winter approaches."We need support, most importantly with machinery, equipment, among others. Our colleagues here don't have [engine] oil and spare parts to continue to work with all the equipment that is still in Gaza."The UN's humanitarian relief co-ordinator, Ramiz Alakbarov, said he was "devastated" by the reports of the building collapse."No-one should have to risk their life simply to find a safe place to shelter," he said.He also urged Israeli authorities to approve deliveries to Gaza of heavy machinery for rescue operations, as well as tents, tarpaulins and other non-food items for displaced people ahead of the winter rains.Israel says its restrictions are meant to keep equipment out of the hands of Palestinian armed groups that could also have military uses.Image source, ReutersImage caption, About 1.2 million people in Gaza are currently living in tents or makeshift sheltersAn estimated 80% of all structures in Gaza have been destroyed or damaged during the war between Israel and Hamas, according to the UN.More than 1.9 million people - about 90% of the territory's population - have been displaced, many of them multiple times, and 1.2 million of them are currently living in tents or makeshift shelters, it says.The UN has warned that the humanitarian situation in Gaza remains dire despite the ceasefire agreed last October, as Israeli air strikes and other attacks continue to hit populated areas, causing casualties and property damage and driving further displacement.On Tuesday, Israeli air strikes killed at least five Palestinians, including two children and a Hamas commander, according to health officials and Hamas sources.The Israeli military said it killed a Hamas commander in southern Gaza and another fighter in the north. In both cases, a child was also reportedly killed.Separately, the British charity Medical Aid for Palestinians said that a patient was killed by an Israeli drone at a health centre it supports in Jabalia in northern Gaza. A spokesperson for the Israeli military told the BBC it was not aware of such an incident.The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.Since then, more than 73,790 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

schema.headline: At least 21 killed after war-damaged Gaza building collapses

title: What's gone wrong for Chelsea talent Kendry Paez?
description: Attacking midfielder Kendry Paez has finally pulled on a Chelsea shirt, three years after agreeing a move to Stamford Bridge - albeit for the club's U
body: Attacking midfielder Kendry Paez has finally pulled on a Chelsea shirt, three years after agreeing a move to Stamford Bridge - albeit for the club's Under-21s.Chelsea agreed a £17.27m deal to sign Paez from Ecuadorian side Independiente del Valle in 2023 when he was 16, but his development has not progressed as quickly as many expected.Now 19, Paez made his first appearance in Chelsea colours for Cobham Next Gen, the club's newly-renamed Under-21 side, as a 12th-minute substitute in a 4-1 win away to Arsenal on Saturday.It comes after new manager Xabi Alonso said the midfielder was "not in my plans" and Chelsea listed him as an academy player on the club website.Chelsea explored the possibility of a loan move in English football, but Fifa regulations left the club unable to send him overseas after using all six of their available international loan slots.With 27 caps for Ecuador, an appearance at this summer's World Cup and a reputation as one of South America's brightest young talents alongside Blues team-mate Estevao Willian, what has happened to Paez?Paez is a record breaker and a headline maker.He became the youngest debutant and goalscorer in Ecuadorian top-flight history at the age of 15 before making his debut in the Copa Libertadores, South America's equivalent of the Champions League, later that same season.Later in 2023, aged 16 years and 131 days, he made his second appearance for Ecuador, becoming the second-youngest South American international to feature in World Cup qualifying after Diego Maradona. A month later, he became the youngest South American to score in a World Cup qualifier in a 2-1 win away to Bolivia.It was understandable, therefore, that Chelsea believed the attacker, who had two international goals and 18 caps when they agreed to sign him, was destined for big things.Chelsea allowed him to train regularly with the first team before he was officially eligible to join the club following his 18th birthday.They also provided security for Paez, his family and the family of international team-mate Moises Caicedo after violence broke out in Ecuador in early 2024.A few months later, Paez was filmed in a New York strip club while away on international duty.He initially impressed on loan at Chelsea's sister club Strasbourg by winning September's Young Player of the Month award in the French top flight, but then came in for criticism from then-manager Liam Rosenior."We expect more, clearly," Rosenior said later that season. "I'm tired of using the excuse of the player's youth."Despite Strasbourg's links to Chelsea through their shared ownership, the loan was cut short after one goal in 21 appearances. Instead, he joined Argentine giants River Plate on a two-year loan spell.Sources in Argentina expressed similar concerns about his attitude when asked by BBC Sport. They point to a disappointing display in the 1-0 Superclasico defeat by fierce rivals Boca Juniors at the Monumental in April.Shortly afterwards, Paez was named by club president Stefano Di Carlo as one of 15 players training away from River Plate's first team, although other sources felt he could have been given more opportunities.His loan ended by mutual consent after Paez scored once in 14 appearances in 461 minutes for River Plate.Ahead of the international break, concern has been expressed in Ecuador, having built him up as the country's next great attacking talent. Michel Deller, the owner of Independiente, told Hincha Amarillo: "He's like a son to us. We care about him deeply. "He's a good kid who's had a tough time and has made decisions that have complicated his life. "We are always hopeful he'll show his exceptional talent one again but right now, it's up to him to decide what to do with his life."These concerns are not dismissed completely by Chelsea or Paez's environment. However, there is a belief they are grossly overstated, highlighting he is owed time to grow as a player and person. There was one reminder of Paez's quality in the dying moments of Cobham Next Gen's (Chelsea Under-21s) defeat at Wycombe Wanderers in the EFL Trophy on Tuesday.It was an outswinging cross from a short corner routine, which Harrison Bettoni tapped in during added time. He then put in another cross that caused havoc as Chelsea chased an equaliser in front of just 778 fans. It was a much-needed boost for Spanish-speaking Paez, who appeared to stand alone from the other academy players before kick-off.He did join in their warm-ups but mostly kept to himself before coming on in the 62nd minute. Ultimately Chelsea lost, while Paez was a peripheral figure playing as a right-sided No 10, like Cole Palmer, in a system that mirrored Alonso's back-three shape. That was until his flurry of activity late on. Although he's not Chelsea's youngest player, Paez has already made 70 appearances for Ecuadorian side Independiente and more than 100 senior matches in total.It's something he can fall back on in a more than salvageable situation. Chelsea have been encouraged by his attitude, having him back in the building at Cobham where he has trained in a stable and elite environment. There is stability around him as family attended his recent match at Wycombe. The Blues are also now able to monitor his development more closely, while academy matches are regularly attended by scouts from across the English Football League and beyond.There is optimism from those close to Paez that he can impress and gain a first loan move in England in January, or one of the six international loan spots will become available for him to go overseas again. It's more than possible he can rediscover the form that attracted Chelsea in the first place and fulfil the immense potential that made him one of South America's most coveted young talents.

schema.headline: What's gone wrong for Chelsea talent Kendry Paez?

title: Ed Sheeran row: How being music's Mr Nice Guy contributed to biggest crisis of his career
description: Figure caption, Will Ed Sheeran cancel his tour as support acts quit?ByMusic correspondentSinger Ed Sheeran is facing the biggest controversy of his c
body: Figure caption, Will Ed Sheeran cancel his tour as support acts quit?ByMusic correspondentSinger Ed Sheeran is facing the biggest controversy of his career after a storm over a decision to drop support act Macklemore from his US stadium tour following the rapper's on-stage pro-Palestinian comments.Sheeran is one of the most successful songwriters of all time. He has sold more than 120 million records and spent more than 1,000 weeks on the US album charts.Part of his appeal - apart from those insidiously catchy songs - is his everyman persona. He looks and dresses like a fan on the train home from Glastonbury, rather than one of the festival's headliners.He has carefully cultivated a non-threatening, everyone welcome public image. In 2014, he donated his entire wardrobe to charity shops. The same year, he adopted a one-month-old kitten, saving it from euthanasia, and named it Graham. Today, he runs a charity providing music lessons to under-18s in his home county of Suffolk.He tries to stay out of politics - usually only getting involved to campaign for issues like copyright protection and ticket touting, or to raise concerns over the impact of Brexit on touring musicians.But like most artists, he leans left. In 2017, he said he supported then-Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, despite not endorsing him at the stump."People thought that, because I didn't put myself behind him, I wasn't a Corbyn supporter," Sheeran told the Sunday Times. "If you knew me as a person, and listened to my music, you would be able to make a pretty educated guess that he would be the kind of person I really dig."When it comes to non-musical issues, Sheeran prefers to remain circumspect. His reasoning, he says, is that music should unite. He views his concerts as a "place of safety and sanctuary" built on shared humanity.This week, that argument has come crumbling down - creating a crisis for his reputation and career.Image source, Shaun Whitmore/BBCBy now, you probably know the story. Macklemore was picked as opening act on Sheeran's US tour, and on the first night made a speech saying "Free Palestine" and showing images of the destruction in Gaza.The following night, he referred to the death toll as a genocide, a claim that Israel rejects.He faced condemnation, with the organisation StopAntisemitism accusing Macklemore of "ambushing" the audience. Stadium owners, apparently led by the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots, Robert Kraft, put pressure on Sheeran and his promoters to drop him from the tour.After a week of backroom discussions, they got their way.On Tuesday, Sheeran issued a statement saying the decision was made by the promoters, not by him.He said he had tried to build bridges between the parties, to no avail. And he said he was "not complicit", arguing that his decision to remain out of the Middle East debate in public wasn't proof he "didn't care"."I am appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine," he wrote. "The suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy. There are too many wars across the world causing immeasurable pain, none of which should be tolerated."He continued: "There is a reason I do not use my professional platform for politics - my audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds."The statement landed with a thud.If Sheeran is so concerned about children, critics said, how come he hasn't mentioned the thousands of children killed in Gaza?Others pointed out that his abstention from politics was not absolute. He wore a "justice for Grenfell" T-shirt at Wembley Stadium in 2018 after the Grenfell Tower fire, played the Concert For Ukraine in 2022, and recorded a protest song about the Ukraine war with U2 earlier this year.Questions were also raised about his relationship with Kraft. Sheeran sang at the businessman's wedding in 2022, and in a subsequent interview called him "super sweet".Music journalist Jeffrey Ingold said Sheeran's apparent acceptance of the decision to drop Macklemore seemed like "cowardice"."He is one of the biggest musicians in the world," Ingold told BBC Radio 5 Live. "He has power and he has leverage. And he has essentially washed his hands and said, this is not my responsibility."He had options, right? He could have said to the promoters and the owners of the venues, including Robert Kraft, 'You know what, we're not going to do the shows there. If you're not going to let us all perform, we're not going to do it'. He could have found alternate venues."Hours after Sheeran's statement landed, his tour went into crisis. All three support acts for the remaining shows - Finneas, Aaron Rowe and Lukas Graham - pulled out, voicing support for Macklemore. Beoga - who back Sheeran to play songs like Galway Girl and Nancy Mulligan - also quit.Many of them said Macklemore's axing, at the hands of a group of billionaire venue owners, represented a chilling effect on free speech.Others from music and beyond have spoken out. Pop star Pink, who is Jewish, reposted an anti-Macklemore meme and then her own message, explaining why she was critical of the rapper's comments.Suddenly, against his will, Sheeran has become the centre of a political storm over one of the world's most divisive issues.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Ed Sheeran performing with Macklemore at the iHeartRadio Music Festival in 2014Could Sheeran have handled it better when the controversy blew up? Absolutely.In his statement, he said he wanted to continue the tour, to avoid letting down fans and the crew who rely on his concerts to make a living.If he had threatened to pull the plug on the shows, he could have framed it as a protest for free speech - although that would still inevitably have been interpreted as an endorsement of Macklemore's statements.So, Sheeran stumbled into a Catch 22 situation. He was damned either way.His nice guy image has taken a huge dent, and the "not my responsibility" tone of his statement certainly didn't help.Ingold says: "I think it will change the way people look at him and see him from this point forward."He has said he's not complicit, but he actually is incredibly complicit in what's happening [on this tour]."Jem Aswad, executive music editor of Variety, says the episode shows "you can't be neutral on this issue" - but points out that most people don't go to Sheeran's concerts to be reminded of issues like Gaza, "they go there to stop thinking about it and be entertained".Aswad doubts that this controversy will cause his career major damage, saying he doesn't think most of the criticism "is necessarily coming from Ed Sheeran's fans"."It's coming from people who object to the way that he's behaved in this [situation], and I'm not sure a lot of those people are really Ed Sheeran's fans."We'll find out when Sheeran plays his next show in Philadelphia on Saturday. A vocal contingent might make their thoughts known, but many will just be turning up to enjoy the music.The loss of his backing band isn't the disaster it may seem, either.On previous tours, Sheeran has been the only artist on stage - accompanying himself on a loop pedal instead of relying on other musicians.But once this run of concerts ends in Mexico this December, his next steps will have to be carefully planned.Perhaps, in an age of febrile discontent, staying above the fray is simply impossible.Get in touchAre you an Ed Sheeran fan? Get in touch.

schema.headline: Ed Sheeran row: How being music's Mr Nice Guy contributed to biggest crisis of his career

title: Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings
description: Figure caption, Why is Donald Trump so opposed to regulating AI?ByNorth America correspondentAccording to Donald Trump, concerns about the dangers of
body: Figure caption, Why is Donald Trump so opposed to regulating AI?ByNorth America correspondentAccording to Donald Trump, concerns about the dangers of artificial intelligence technology – that "robots will be marching into our cities and getting rid of us all" – are a hoax.It's the kind of language the US president typically reserves for the objects of his most intense derision – theories about human-driven climate change, investigations into Russian election-meddling, and the drives to impeach and remove him from office during his first presidential term.Styling himself as the "hoax buster", in a series of social media posts on Monday he issued a full-throated endorsement of what he called "the greatest economic development engine in history" and scorned those who doubted the benefits of the technology.The ranks of doubters have been growing in recent weeks, however, amidst anxiety over the disruptive nature of AI - if not worries about potentially civilisation-threatening danger - among some industry insiders and politicians, including from within Trump's own Republican Party.None of that has deterred Trump, however, whose latest social media fusillade was only his latest effort to turn back growing AI scepticism through sheer force of will. Whether the president views the AI fight as pivotal to his economic legacy, a key battleground in a global struggle for power, or another example of his enemies conspiring against him, he has, by fully joining the fight, elevated the issue to the forefront of American politics. That is even at the risk of crossing longtime allies."We think this could be a great technology, but we're not going to give these guys a carte blanche," former Trump adviser Steve Bannon said at a "pro-human" conference on the dangers of AI on Tuesday. "There's been no debate."Just before Bannon spoke, democratic socialist Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont told the same crowd that Washington policymakers had not addressed the "potentially catastrophic consequence" of unregulated AI."Congress under both Democratic and Republican control has been asleep at the wheel," he said. "And now we have a president whose ignorance regarding this issue is truly embarrassing."Figure caption, Watch: "Great" or "alarming" - Should AI be reined in?According to Trump, however, what's needed isn't debate or new policies, it's trust in his authority and judgement."The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades," he wrote. "We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies."A desire for centralised presidential authority is a familiar theme for Trump in his second term in office. If he decides something is good, he should have the authority to allow it; if he deems it bad, he ought to be able to end it by unilateral presidential order.It's similar to his outlook on immigration and trade. He believes that he, as president, should have the sole power to decide who can enter and remain in the country, and when and where to impose tariffs.Unlike tariffs and immigration, which have been issues of interest for Trump for decades, the rise in artificial intelligence technology is a recent development.But if this is no long-time, deep-seated interest on the part of the president, what could explain his willingness to press ahead?The 'hottest' economy and the driving force of AITrump regularly likes to tout America as the "hottest" country in the world. Many economists indicate that investment in AI technology – including infrastructure and equipment – has been the driving force in the US economy for several years. According to a recent report by the forecasting firm ING, tech investment accounted for more than a third of all US economic expansion in the second quarter of 2026.The stock market is booming, and much of that rise in corporate value (and, by extension, surging retirement portfolios of many Americans) can be attributed to the massive spending on computer chips, data centres and the other infrastructure behind AI.Anything that threatens this growth, which Trump considers to be a hallmark of his presidency and a key to his political legacy, quickly draws his suspicion.Trump also sees the AI expansion as a large-scale industrial competition between the world's two largest economies, the US and China. In the zero-sum game of global power, if China is ahead, then America is behind."We're leading China in AI," Trump said on Saturday, "and frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI wins."The president often touts a familiar conservative view that his opponents on the left are against the free market and economic liberties, and rely on alarmism to justify greater government intervention and control.Of course, Trump – who touts partial US ownership of US Steel and the semiconductor manufacturer Intel, and has no qualms about picking winners and losers in the American economy – is hardly a traditional small-government conservative.Tech bosses vary in views - and their access to TrumpTrump's close ties to prominent tech moguls and AI entrepreneurs from the start of his second term may also help explain his AI evangelism. Tech entrepreneur David Sacks, a co-chair of the president's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology and his informal AI tsar, has been a longtime supporter. Sacks's publicly aired scepticism of AI regulation mirrors recent comments made by the president."I think this is becoming a panic," he said this weekend in an interview with CBS News. "We're in an election season, and there is an incentive for political actors to try and amplify the fear."Elon Musk, despite a rocky relationship, has shaped the direction of this administration. Mark Zuckerberg of Facebook, Amazon's Jeff Bezos, OpenAI's Sam Altman and former Apple head Tim Cook all had prominent seats at Trump's inauguration.These men, along with Anthropic head Dario Amodei, hold a range of views on the necessity of greater AI regulation, and have differing levels of access to, and influence on, Trump.In Amodei's case, his conflicts over the Pentagon's unrestricted use of Anthropic's AI models could have negatively affected Trump's evaluation of Amodei's calls for a slowdown in AI development."This is the most prominent debate in the entire industry and has been since the beginning," said Matt Calkins, head of the tech firm Appian. "We knew it would spill into politics at some point because it had to."Figure caption, Watch: AI needs a 'brake pedal', Anthropic co-founder tells BBCWhere the political debate goes from here is an open question.With Trump's resistance, it is unlikely that Congress – despite promises of new hearings and proposed regulatory controls – will enact new legislation that Trump would sign into law. On Tuesday, Republican Speaker of the House Mike Johnson appeared to back away from earlier openness to congressional action, instead echoing Trump "AI hoax" rhetoric.With midterm congressional elections looming, candidates running for office – both Republicans and Democrats – are wary of ending up on the wrong side of public opinion that, according to polls, is sceptical of the promised benefits of AI advances.But Republicans are also wary of crossing Trump on an issue that has become a political touchstone for the president.Even though the public is starting to pay attention, Calkins says that the issue has not yet become political dynamite, which means political rhetoric comes with little risk. The moment when AI warnings turn into a high-profile disaster, however, could be looming."It is possible that events in the future might electrify the public, and then positions - and talk - might not be so cheap," he said.Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's weekly US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

title: Former Cambridgeshire officer jailed for 'toxic' WhatsApp culture
description: In the autumn of 2020, Williams was tasked with examining the phone of a female suspect he told Street was "quite fit".Street asked him if there were
body: In the autumn of 2020, Williams was tasked with examining the phone of a female suspect he told Street was "quite fit".Street asked him if there were "any nudes", and Williams replied there was a video of the woman committing a sexual act. Williams went on to send Street a photo from the woman's phone.The following year, Street asked on WhatsApp if Williams still had the intimate private video because he wanted to show it to "the lads from footy".Reading her victim personal statement in court, the woman said: "The photographs and videos on my phone were deeply private and intimate."Learning that people in positions of authority deliberately accessed and circulated these images has left me feeling exposed, degraded and powerless."Mitigating, Jennifer Dempster KC said Street "enormously regrets his behaviour", adding: "He recognises he has not only let the public down, he has let the police down and he has let his family down."For Williams, Robert Morris said: "He recognises what he did was deeply inappropriate, driven by misguided and stupid desire to engage in salacious gossip."Senior specialist prosecutor Lisa Rose, from the CPS, said: "Police officers are entrusted with significant powers and are expected to uphold the highest standards at all times."The actions of Paul Street and Joshua Williams represented a serious breach of that trust."Do you have a story suggestion for Cambridgeshire? Contact us below.

title: VAR controversy: Pressure for quick decisions obvious in rushed derby review
description: "Quick, quick, quick, quick! Go, go, go, go, go!"The words of video assistant referee Matt Donohue as he rushed through the review to award Erling Haa
body: "Quick, quick, quick, quick! Go, go, go, go, go!"The words of video assistant referee Matt Donohue as he rushed through the review to award Erling Haaland's winning goal in the Manchester derby.No doubt Donohue was simply trying to be as efficient as possible, but it led to one of the most catastrophic VAR errors the Premier League has seen. Donohue and his assistant VAR, Blake Antrobus, inexplicably failed to notice that Enzo Fernandez was three yards offside before he tried to head the ball.The goal was given, and Manchester City beat Manchester United 1-0. Refereeing has always been a goldfish bowl of scrutiny and pressure, heightened by the introduction of VAR.The Premier League made a "more efficient application of VAR to reduce delays" one of its football principles for the season.Has the game tried to prioritise speed over accuracy? The urgency in Donohue's voice was all too apparent. "Let's go, let's go, let's go, let's go!"It was a panicked exchange between the VAR and the replay operator. Not calm, collected and methodical. Rushed and chaotic. The opposite of how a video official should operate.Officials hear repeatedly - from fans, pundits, radio phone-ins and newspaper columns - that VAR has to be quicker. That delays are not acceptable.In the Premier League stakeholders' survey - which includes managers, coaches and supporters - the key theme for improvements to VAR was the speed of decisions.This has to create pressure - but it is no excuse for such an error.City boss Enzo Maresca had some sympathy speaking on Wednesday, though he was of course the beneficiary of the gaffe."To make a decision in 10, 20 seconds is not easy for them," said Maresca. "Sometimes they make mistakes. I make mistakes, players make mistakes. It's part of our job."Referees' chief Howard Webb has taken the desire for quicker reviews on board, but it is still a balancing act.There has been a positive impact, as far as the stats go.VAR delays - including the referee making an announcement to the crowd - have been reduced, from an average of 46 seconds per game to 36 seconds season-on-season. Yet the only other VAR mistake, the failure to award a penalty to Arsenal at Aston Villa, also arguably came about because the incident was cleared too quickly.Completing a VAR review in the shortest possible time is not about skipping steps. And it was a critical mistake by Donohue and Antrobus.Speed is a factor, but the most serious error in process came before Donohue tried to rush through the attacking phase.Donohue asked the replay operator to stop the video on the first replay when Josko Gvardiol touched the ball to cross into the area. He then went immediately into the semi-automated offside technology.This should not have happened.The VAR team should have assessed the full picture, from the playing of the cross to the head of Haaland. This would have provided awareness of Fernandez's position and impact.They did not, and the events inside the penalty area were not considered until the attacking phase was looked at.By then, all that mattered to Donohue and Antrobus was whether Fernandez touched the ball. This would have created a new phase and placed Haaland offside. Donohue has received much of the criticism, but arguably Antrobus' involvement, or lack of, was just as influential.The AVAR's contribution to the entire review was to utter "no, yeah" about the potential touch by Fernandez. This was one second before Donohue uttered the words "final decision is goal, check complete".Antrobus' role is to provide the checks and balances, to make sure the VAR has not missed anything. This fell short. There has been only one lengthy VAR delay this season, in the game between Brentford and Sunderland. A Dan Ballard goal was ruled out for a subjective offside against Kevin Danso.Antrobus was the AVAR in this game, too. There was a great deal of criticism in some parts of the media for that delay, which took over four minutes.Could that have played on Antrobus' mind on Sunday? We cannot know for sure. Ironically, Antrobus played a crucial role in steering VAR Tim Wood to the correct offside decision against Danso. There is also the role of the support VAR, who sits in the operations room next to the match hub at Stockley Park and can intervene on points on protocol.Aware of what was unfolding with the review, no action was taken.It would still have been salvageable in the period between the goal being scored and the kick-off.Pro Ref has placed a huge level of training and resources into VAR in an attempt to make it as efficient and accurate as possible.But when an error of this magnitude happens, no amount of investment can mask the failure. There have been calls to appoint VAR specialists, yet this is exactly what Donohue is - in the Premier League's definition. Three seasons ago, Pro Ref asked for candidates interested in becoming video officials. All those who applied were put through aptitude tests. About 15 made it through to the final stages of training, of which 10 have officiated games in the Premier League.One of those is Donohue, who on Sunday was the video official for the 65th time.Such as been Donohue's development that he is now on the international list, appointed to Uefa club competition qualifying ties over the summer. Donohue has made mistakes, in fact very few do not. It shows how difficult the role is. The only two VARs to have a clear record over the last two seasons are Nick Hopton and Neil Davies, both graduates from the same accelerated programme.Persuading referees to hang up their whistles and spend their professional lives in the VAR room is not easy, nor does it guarantee success.Lee Mason and Mike Dean, the Premier League's only full-time VARs appointed after retirement, were both dismissed by Webb just a few months into his tenure because of a catalogue of errors.One of the only leagues which has a full team of officials who only act as VARs and never go out on the pitch is Spain's La Liga and second division - yet one glance at the headlines there will tell you the controversy is no different to that in England.At the start of last season the VAR completely missed that a player who scored a goal was in an offside position when the ball was played.Pro Ref will have questions to answer over its processes and why a VAR is rushing so desperately over a review in one of the biggest games of the season.That did not happen when West Ham's stoppage-time equaliser against Arsenal was ruled out last season. It took over four minutes - but the VAR came to the correct outcome.The obsession with speed threatens to undermine all the work behind the scenes. But that feels like a football problem and not one caused solely by the actions of the VAR.

schema.headline: VAR controversy: Pressure for quick decisions obvious in rushed derby review

title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teacher pay strike
description: Schools in England are to get around £500 million in extra funding towards the teachers' pay award this school year, reducing the risk of a strike bal
body: Schools in England are to get around £500 million in extra funding towards the teachers' pay award this school year, reducing the risk of a strike ballot by the largest education union.Schools had been expected to fund some of the 3.5% teachers pay increase for the current school year out of their existing budgets, which National Education Union (NEU) leaders had strongly objected to.Daniel Kebede, the General Secretary of the NEU, said the offer of more funding was a "significant" step in negotiations.In a letter to the union on Wednesday, which has been seen by the BBC, the government said the increase would be funded by savings in employers' contributions to the local government pension scheme.The letter said the 4.9 percentage point drop in what employers are expected to contribute will deliver "significant savings" on the pay bill for support staff, which will not be clawed back by central government.The National Education Union said it expected the extra money to be around £500m, which schools can now use towards teachers pay this year.In July, ministers accepted the recommendation of the independent pay review body for teachers and agreed a 3.5% increase from September 2026 would be followed by 3% the following year.The pay increase had been partly funded by an additional £700m for 2026-27 and £1.1bn for the following year.Independent economists at the Institute for Fiscal Studies said that left schools facing a shortfall of around 1% between rising costs and funding this year.The additional money could potentially bring the uplift for this year into line with next year.Kebede said schools has been "running on empty" and the funding signalled "a welcome return to reality, and a message of hope for the entire school community".In an indicative ballot by the NEU in April, 90% of teachers who voted said they would be prepared to take industrial action over funding and pay, on a turnout of 48%.A formal ballot was due to begin on 3 October and close 15 December, raising the prospects of teachers pay strikes early in 2027.The national executive of the NEU will meet on 24 September to consider whether to call that off following the additional funding on offer from the government.

schema.headline: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teacher pay strike

title: EU chief backs plan for Canada to become 'associate member'
description: The president of the European Commission has backed proposals for Canada to become the EU's first "associate member".Ursula von der Leyen told the Eur
body: The president of the European Commission has backed proposals for Canada to become the EU's first "associate member".Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament on Wednesday she wanted to work on "opening the door" for Canada, which would involve closer ties on various key sectors.Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney last week spoke of seeking a "unique alliance" with the EU. The country currently faces tense relations with the US, compounded by an intensifying dispute over trade.Without mentioning US President Donald Trump by name, von der Leyen said offering Canada some sort of EU membership was "not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength". She added: "Partnerships are a strategic choice for Europe. But they also respond to the fracture in the international rules-based system".Carney was in attendance at the annual key note speech in Strasbourg, and is due to address the parliament on Thursday.Trade talks between Canada and the US collapsed last month, sparking a series of new tariff measures. Trump's repeated talk of making Canada a "51st state" has also helped to fuel the feud between the North American neighbours.Von der Leyen told the EU's State of the Union address that the bloc and Canada "see the world with the same eyes", including on topics ranging from AI, to climate change and geopolitics."And we have stood together: on Ukraine, on defence, on raw materials and on supply chains. But above all... Europe and Canada believe in democracy."She did not give specific details on how any Canadian membership would work, but listed manufacturing, technology, AI, defence, energy, critical minerals and economic security as key areas for cooperation.Both she and other European leaders have found a reliable ally in Carney as they deal with similar problems.In particular, they have faced Trump's aggressive use of tariffs and his threat to annex Greenland which is a sovereign territory of EU member Denmark.But "associate membership" of the EU does not currently exist and the process, if agreed, could take years.Earlier this year, Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz suggested - to a mixed reaction - that Ukraine could be granted this new status.Some countries in the western Balkans including Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, and Serbia are already on the long road towards full EU membership.In Eastern Europe, Georgia and Moldova are also applying.Ten of the bloc's 27 members are yet to ratify a free-trade agreement struck with Ottawa nearly a decade ago, and some capitals would prefer to build on existing defence and trade agreements rather than create a new form of membership for Canada.Setting out the EU's political and policy priorities for year ahead, von der Leyen also proposed the formation of a European Security Council, which would include the UK and Ukraine, amid an ongoing threat to the continent from Russia. "For a long time, we have discussed a leaders' format focused on the security of our continent, with partners like Canada, Norway, Ukraine, the United Kingdom and others involved," she said in the wide-ranging address."This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play. This is why we will set out our ideas to make a European Security Council a reality."Calls for such a body have been growing since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.It was initially a French-German conception but more countries have shown support, particularly as Trump has questioned the Nato military alliance. Other nations worry such a council could unhelpfully rival Nato.Von der Leyen said the EU was "strengthening our work with Nato" and that expanded defence spending would be "fully aligned" with the alliance.But at the core of such a security council would be the ability to trigger an emergency meeting if one member felt under threat, similar to Nato's Article 4.The EU chief said it would be a "mechanism to flank" Article 4, a term that could be interpreted as complementing Nato functions or - if taken in a military context - bypassing them.Alongside global threats, von der Leyen also said many European families were worried about the cost of living, and the "dizzying speed of change" of technology and its impacts on jobs and society.Other proposals included inviting the world's largest AI labs for talks on how to support industry efforts to pace the frontier, as well as slashing bureaucracy for businesses in the EU. Plans to curb social media use among children, including banning platforms for under 13s, were also put forward. Under the proposal, children aged 13 to 15 would only be able to set up social media accounts which are supervised by parents.A new emergency tool to help countries better deal with mass migration movements following the deadly influx of migrants to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in July would also be outlined.The pledge chimes with the message of European politicians on the right and hard right who have gained support in recent years for proposing a tougher approach.Some of them called the mass attempt to enter the EU through Ceuta an "invasion" and argued asylum rules should be suspended to deal with such a crisis.Von der Leyen said the new emergency tool would "only be triggered under a strictly defined set of criteria" and for a specific period of time, and that fundamental rights would be protected.Human rights groups worry such a move would see vulnerable people, including women and children, turned back and denied the protection afforded to them under international law.

schema.headline: EU chief backs plan for Canada to become 'associate member'

title: Photos show widespread damage at US sites from Iranian attacks
description: Image source, CBS NewsImage caption, An undated photo shows a car reportedly destroyed in an Iranian strike at Camp Buehring in KuwaitByKayla EpsteinI
body: Image source, CBS NewsImage caption, An undated photo shows a car reportedly destroyed in an Iranian strike at Camp Buehring in KuwaitByKayla EpsteinImages showing widespread damage to multiple US sites in the Middle East from Iranian strikes have been obtained by the BBC's US partner CBS.The photos, provided by active military personnel, show a severed radar jet, flattened trailers and severely damaged buildings.The undated photos were taken at US bases and sites in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait.One member of the military, who was not named by CBS, said: "This is major damage to our bases that hasn't been communicated to the American public."We're standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face."The White House and US Central Command have been approached for comment.The photos, which have not been independently verified by the BBC, were published the day after a report from the Pentagon's watchdog confirmed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in the Middle East have been damaged and destroyed by Iran.One of the photos showed a destroyed Boeing E-3 Sentry at Prince Sultan Air Force Base in Saudi Arabia that has been ripped in half, its tail section crumpled into a tangled mess of metal.Image source, CBS NewsImage caption, An undated photo of a destroyed Boeing E-3 Sentry at Prince Sultan air base in Saudi Arabia, about 62 miles (100km) south-east of the capital RiyadhWhile the photo is undated, BBC Verify previously confirmed a similar photo, apparently of the same radar aircraft in March.The Boeing E-3 Awacs are used to detect and track potential targets at long ranges to provide an early warning of possible threats.At the time, a US official told Reuters that 12 US personnel had been wounded, two of them seriously, in an Iranian attack on the air base.A pair of undated images reportedly from Camp Beuhring, Kuwait, show crumpled trailers, and a large tent-like structure that had been reduced to shreds as smoke billowed from the site.Image source, CBS NewsImage caption, Trailers destroyed by Iranian strike at Camp Buehring, KuwaitImage source, CBS NewsImage caption, Undated photo shows smoke billowing from a structure that sustained damage in an Iranian strike at Camp Buehring, KuwaitAnother image shows a four-storey building damaged by an Iranian strike at Camp Arifjan, in Kuwait.Damage to the site was reported in March, including on satellite communications hardware, though it is not clear whether this image is from the same attack.Image source, CBS NewsImage caption, Damage to a building can be seen in this photo from Camp Arifjan, KuwaitThe images were published on the heels of a report from the Pentagon's watchdog, which found Iranian strikes had "damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan during the conflict".It also noted that equipment losses have totalled $3.7bn (£2.8bn). Overall, the US spent $33.4bn (£24.7bn) on the war up to 29 June, the report said.In the months after the war began, "dozens of US aircraft were destroyed or damaged", the report continues.The document lists several of the aircraft damaged, including five refuelling aircraft which were "damaged or destroyed on the ground in Saudi Arabia by Iranian munitions".Figure caption, Watch: What does the munitions shortage mean for the US?Public and political pressure has mounted on the White House to find an end to the conflict with Iran, which began on 28 February when the US and Israel launched joint attacks on the country.Since the war began Iran has repeatedly attacked US bases and allied states in the Gulf, as well as Israel.On Tuesday night, the US House of Representatives voted for the third time to end the war in Iran, approving a measure that would force President Donald Trump to end US military action without congressional approval. The vote passed with the help of several Republicans, in what is likely to be the final such House vote ahead of the US midterm elections in November.

schema.headline: Photos show widespread damage at US sites from Iranian attacks
